items.title: Ballots Already Mailed, Map Still in Dispute: Inside Missouri's Redistricting Fight at the Supreme Court
items.body:
Missouri voters are starting to receive and return ballots for the November 3 election. The congressional map those ballots are based on may not be the one that ends up being used.

A federal appeals court has ordered Missouri to use a Republican-drawn congressional map that dissolves a Kansas City-based Democratic district. The order came even though ballots reflecting the older district lines had already been printed and mailed. On Tuesday night, the dispute went back to the U.S. Supreme Court, the third time in September that the justices have been asked to step in.

This article explains what happened, what each side argues, and what is still unsettled. The situation is changing quickly, and details are current as of September 24, 2026.

## The short version

- **What is being fought over:** Which of two congressional maps Missouri uses in the November 2026 general election. One is the 2022 map. The other is a map passed by the Republican-led legislature in 2025.
- **Who is affected most directly:** Voters in and around Kansas City. The 2025 map dismantles the 5th Congressional District, which Democratic U.S. Rep. Emanuel Cleaver II holds.
- **Where things stand:** The 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals ruled on Monday, September 21 that the 2025 map must be used. That ruling is paused until Monday, September 28 to give the Supreme Court time to act.
- **What happens next:** The justices could block the order, let it take effect, or extend the pause while they consider the case.

## How the dispute got here

The fight has moved through state and federal courts in a short time. Here is the sequence as reported by news outlets:

- **2025:** Missouri Republicans passed a new congressional map as part of a wider national push, backed by President Donald Trump, to redraw U.S. House districts in ways that favor Republican candidates. The map reshapes the Kansas City-area district represented by Cleaver.
- **Referendum petition:** A group called People Not Politicians gathered signatures for a referendum that would let voters decide whether the new map should take effect. Its position is that the map cannot be used until voters weigh in.
- **August 4:** Missouri held its party primaries using the 2025 map. State officials argued that the referendum petition had not yet been certified.
- **September 3:** The Missouri Supreme Court unanimously ruled that, under state law, the 2025 map could not be used in this year's midterms until it goes to a referendum. It directed officials to use the 2022 map.
- **Early September:** The U.S. Supreme Court declined to take up an appeal from Missouri officials. Hours later, a federal district judge in St. Louis, Stephen Clark, issued a temporary order barring any map other than the 2025 one. A few days after that, the Supreme Court stayed his order, which restored the instruction to use the 2022 map.
- **September 21:** A three-judge panel of the 8th Circuit sided with the 2025 map and ordered its use. Judge Clark then issued an order to that effect but delayed it until September 28 so appeals could proceed.
- **Late Tuesday, September 22:** People Not Politicians asked the Supreme Court to block the federal order. Justice Brett Kavanaugh, who handles emergency matters from the 8th Circuit, set a deadline for responses on Wednesday.

## Why the appeals court ruled the way it did

According to reporting on the decision, the 8th Circuit's reasoning turned on a constitutional argument about consistency within a single election cycle. Voters, the court said, should elect members of Congress in districts that match the ones used in the primary. The August primary was held under the 2025 map, so switching to the 2022 map for November would place roughly 284,000 primary voters in different districts for the general election.

The panel wrote that "only use of the 2025 map complies with the Constitution and federal law." It also noted that during the campaign, Missourians "filed to run for Congress, met candidates, watched campaign advertisements, received campaign mail, and voted under the 2025 map."

The court also addressed the Purcell principle. This is a doctrine courts often cite for avoiding late changes to election rules that could confuse voters and election workers. The panel reportedly treated the 2025 map, which the primary was run on, as the practical status quo. It therefore rejected the argument that the doctrine blocked its order.

## What the other side says

People Not Politicians and other supporters of the 2022 map see it differently. They point to the Missouri Supreme Court's ruling on how the state's own referendum process works. They also note that the U.S. Supreme Court has already acted twice this month in ways that left the 2022 map in place.

The group's executive director, Richard von Glahn, has argued that map changes in the middle of an election are the real problem. "You cannot change maps in the middle of an election," he said, expressing confidence in the group's position.

Supporters of the 2025 map, including Missouri's secretary of state and Republican candidates running under the new lines, argue that the primary results and the campaign activity that followed make the 2025 map the operative one.

## The ballot problem

The timing is what makes this case unusual. Ballots for the November 3 election were printed with the 2022 district lines and mailed, including to overseas and military voters. Absentee voting began this week. If the 2025 map is imposed, election officials would face the task of reissuing or reconciling ballots very close to Election Day. The 8th Circuit's own order said the 2025 map should govern, but neither the courts nor state officials have publicly laid out a complete plan for how ballots would be handled if the order takes effect.

Missouri voters will also see a statewide question on November 3, Proposition A, which asks whether to approve the 2025 map. People Not Politicians is campaigning for a "no" vote. The group has reported spending millions on its signature drive, and a committee called Put Missouri First has spent to oppose it.

## What to watch next

1. **A Supreme Court order before September 28.** Given the deadline, the justices are expected either to rule on the emergency request or to extend the pause.
2. **Guidance for election officials.** Local election authorities will need clear instructions on which districts appear on ballots and how to handle ballots already issued.
3. **The larger legal question.** The case tests how much weight federal courts should give to a state supreme court's reading of state law, and how far the "no late changes" principle reaches when a primary and general election are held under different maps.
4. **The broader House picture.** The Kansas City seat is one of several battlegrounds in a nationwide fight over district lines ahead of the midterms. The outcome could affect the balance of the U.S. House.

## What Missouri voters can do

Because the rules are still unsettled, voters should rely on official sources instead of social media rumors:

- Confirm your registration and your current congressional district with your local election authority or the Missouri Secretary of State's website.
- If you already have an absentee ballot, follow the instructions that came with it and watch for updates from your county election office.
- Check official announcements before returning a ballot, since guidance could change if the courts act.

*This article is a news summary based on publicly reported court filings and coverage. The case is ongoing and details may change.*

items.title: More Than 1 in 5 Middle-Income Renters Missed a Full Rent Payment Last Year, New Urban Institute Report Finds
items.body:
For years, the conversation about rent hardship in America focused mostly on lower-income households. A new report from the Urban Institute suggests the pressure is now reaching much further up the income ladder. According to the organization's latest survey data, roughly 22% of middle-income renters said that at some point in 2025 they could not pay their full rent when it was due.

That is a sharp change from the year before, and it is a bigger jump than the one seen among lower-income renters. Here is what the findings say, who is affected, and why researchers are paying close attention.

## The Key Numbers

The findings come from the Urban Institute's Well-Being and Basic Needs Survey, which asked more than 10,000 adults about how they are managing everyday costs. The share of renters who said they were unable to pay the full amount of rent at least once in the year breaks down as follows:

| Renter group | Earlier figure | 2025 |
|---|---|---|
| Middle-income | about 14% (prior year) | about 22% |
| Lower-income | about 24% (2019) | about 28% |
| Higher-earning | about 5% (prior year) | about 7% |

Two things stand out. First, middle-income renters saw a rise of roughly eight percentage points in a single year. Second, the increase for lower-income renters, while real, has been much more gradual: from about 24% in 2019 to about 28% in 2025. Lower-income renters still report the highest overall rates of trouble paying rent, but the gap between the two groups is narrowing.

## Who Counts as "Middle-Income"?

The report defines middle-income adults by household size. For a single person, that means earning roughly $31,300 to $62,600 a year. For a family of three, the range is roughly $53,300 to $106,600.

Households in these ranges often earn too much to qualify for many housing assistance programs, yet not enough to absorb a sudden jump in rent, a rise in utility bills, or an unexpected expense. That makes them especially exposed when several costs climb at once.

## What "Unable to Pay" Means

In the survey, a renter counts as unable to pay if they could not cover the full amount of rent when it was due. That covers a range of situations, including a late payment, a partial payment, or a missed payment. Not every case ends in a formal eviction filing, and many households catch up later. Still, researchers treat these moments as an early warning sign.

Samantha Batko, a senior fellow at the Urban Institute and a co-author of the report, described the change this way: "This increase among middle-income renters is a big and important shift that reflects overall challenges with affordability in the country." She also noted that when a family reports a late, partial, or missed rent payment, those are choices happening in real time as households try to stretch their budgets.

## A Trend Specific to Renters

The report points to a gap between renters and homeowners. Homeowners' ability to afford their mortgage payments has stayed steady over the past seven years. Rent hardship, by contrast, has been climbing since 2022.

Renters also reported strain beyond the rent itself. More than 20% said they had trouble paying for utilities such as gas, oil, or electricity, which suggests that housing costs are only one part of a broader squeeze on household budgets.

The survey also found that the sharpest increases in missed rent payments during 2025 came in the South and the Northeast.

## Why Researchers Are Concerned

The report ties the trend to mounting economic pressures and the rising cost of everyday necessities. When groceries, transportation, insurance, and utilities all cost more, rent is often the largest bill to come up short.

Batko also raised a longer-term concern about the shift toward middle-income households, noting the potential implications for the number of people who could eventually lose their housing. Households with more income often have more options, such as savings, credit, or help from family, and researchers watch closely for the point where those cushions run out.

## A Note on the Numbers

Reports of this kind rely on self-reported survey responses, so the figures are best read as estimates of how many renters say they struggled, not a count of court filings or formal evictions. Some news coverage has summarized the middle-income finding as "one in five," while the underlying data put it slightly higher, at about 22%. The direction of the trend is clear either way.

## What Renters Can Do

Housing costs are not something any one household can fix alone, but a few practical steps can help anyone who expects to fall behind:

- **Communicate early.** Landlords and property managers are often more willing to discuss a payment plan before a payment is missed than after.
- **Know your local options.** Many cities and counties run emergency rental assistance or mediation programs. Dialing 211 in most areas connects callers to local support services.
- **Seek free housing counseling.** HUD-approved housing counseling agencies offer free or low-cost guidance. A directory is available at hud.gov.
- **Review the lease.** Understanding late-fee rules and notice requirements in your state can help you plan.

## The Bottom Line

The Urban Institute's findings add to a growing body of evidence that housing affordability is no longer only a low-income issue. With about 22% of middle-income renters reporting a missed or incomplete rent payment last year, the strain now reaches households that were once considered financially secure. Whether the trend continues will depend on rents, wages, and the cost of other basics in the months ahead.

*Source: Urban Institute Well-Being and Basic Needs Survey, as reported by [NPR](https://www.npr.org/2026/09/23/nx-s1-5977022/rent-affordability-middle-income) on September 23, 2026. This article is for general information only and does not constitute financial or legal advice.*

items.title: Three Hours, One Ultimatum: Trump's Unannounced Iran Talks After His "Annihilate" Warning at the UN
items.body:
On the same day President Donald Trump told the United Nations General Assembly that Iran faces a stark choice, his envoys sat down for roughly three hours of talks with an Iranian delegation on the sidelines of the summit. The meeting had not been announced beforehand. It came to light when Trump described it to reporters.

The pairing of a blunt public threat with quiet diplomacy shows how U.S.–Iran relations are being handled at a tense moment, nearly seven months into a conflict that has reshaped energy markets and Middle East politics. Here is what is known so far, based on public reporting, and what remains unclear.

## The Warning at the UN

In his address to world leaders, Trump framed the situation as a binary choice. According to reports of the speech, he asked whether he should "annihilate the Islamic Republic" and do so quickly, or whether a negotiated agreement could still be reached. Speaking to reporters afterward, he described the alternatives as "obliteration" on one side and "potential greatness" for Iran on the other.

The language was among the most forceful Trump has used toward Tehran at a multilateral forum. It was also a negotiating position: an ultimatum meant to signal that the window for a deal is limited, and that the alternative is severe.

## The Three-Hour Meeting

Shortly after the speech, Trump said U.S. and Iranian officials had met at the UN General Assembly, and he called the session "very good" and "very productive." Participants named in reports include:

- **Steve Witkoff**, Trump's special envoy
- **Jared Kushner**, Trump's son-in-law and informal adviser
- **Abbas Araghchi**, Iran's foreign minister

Coverage differs on the format. Some accounts describe a face-to-face meeting. At least one report said mediators shuttled between the two sides. The White House and Tehran may give further detail in the coming days. Trump also said another round of talks would take place in the very near future, though no date has been publicly confirmed.

## What Iran Says It Wants

Iranian state broadcaster IRIB said Araghchi laid out Tehran's conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow waterway that carries a large share of the world's seaborne oil. According to that account, Iran is asking for:

- An immediate end to the U.S. naval blockade
- Release of frozen Iranian assets
- An end to the fighting on all fronts, including Lebanon

Washington's stated priorities point in a different direction. Reporting on the talks says the U.S. wants free navigation through the strait and firm limits on Iran's nuclear program. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the administration remained open to further engagement if it could lead to real progress, and he repeated the core U.S. goal that Iran never obtain a nuclear weapon.

## Hard Words on Both Sides

Iran's response to the "annihilate" remark was also defiant. Iran's General Staff said its forces were ready to carry out strikes that would be "more crushing and less predictable" than earlier attacks, according to Al Jazeera.

Analysts caution against reading the rhetoric as a sign that talks are failing. Andreas Krieg of King's College London told Al Jazeera that the escalating language works as a "bargaining strategy," letting each government project strength at home while keeping room to negotiate. On that reading, tough public statements and private meetings are two parts of one process rather than a contradiction.

## The Midterm Factor

Timing is a central question. Trump indicated that a final agreement may not arrive before the November midterm elections, although accounts of his remarks on the timeline have varied slightly, so it is worth watching for clarification.

Domestic politics may be shaping the calendar. The conflict has pushed up U.S. fuel prices, according to Al Jazeera, and energy costs are a sensitive issue for voters. A deal that reopens the Strait of Hormuz could ease that pressure. A deal seen as too generous could draw criticism from opponents in Washington and from U.S. allies in the region. That tension helps explain why both outcomes, a breakthrough and a delay, remain plausible.

## What to Watch Next

- **A second round of talks.** Trump said one is coming soon. Whether it is confirmed, and at what level, will signal how serious the process is.
- **The Strait of Hormuz and the blockade.** Any easing of either would be the clearest sign of progress.
- **Nuclear terms.** Public detail on enrichment limits and inspections has been scarce.
- **Rhetoric versus action.** Watch whether military statements from either side are followed by real escalation or fade as talks continue.

## The Bottom Line

The UN meeting did not produce a deal, and neither side has said it did. It did show that direct or mediated communication between Washington and Tehran is active even as both governments trade sharp warnings in public. Whether that channel leads to an agreement, or whether the ultimatum hardens positions, is likely to become clearer in the weeks before the midterms.

*This article summarizes publicly available reporting as of September 24, 2026. Details of the talks are based on statements from officials and news organizations and may change as the situation develops.*

**Sources:** [The Times of Israel](https://www.timesofisrael.com/us-and-iranian-negotiators-hold-talks-at-un-that-trump-says-went-very-well/), [Al Jazeera](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/9/23/annihilate-vs-crushing-attacks-why-iran-us-up-rhetoric-amid-talks), [Axios](https://www.axios.com/2026/09/22/unga-iran-us-trump-war), [The Week](https://www.theweek.in/news/middle-east/2026/09/23/us-iran-meeting-unga-trump-annihilation-threat.html)

items.title: [Retailing 101 #6] The Aisle in Your Pocket: Retail Without a Store
items.body:
> Non-store retailing doesn't delete the costs of a store — it trades rent and shelf space for shipping, returns, and the price of getting your attention.

## Today's Concept

Every lecture so far has assumed a building: a sales floor, a door, a trade area of people who live close enough to walk in. **Non-store retailing** is everything that sells to final consumers without that floor — direct selling (the Mary Kay rep), automated vending (the machine in the hotel lobby), catalogs and direct mail, TV home shopping, online marketplaces, and mobile commerce.

The three that matter most today are the last three. Here's the useful way to think about them.

A physical store operates under three hard limits:

1. **Shelf space** — a Target carries maybe 80,000 items because that's what fits.
2. **Store hours** — closed at 11 p.m.
3. **Trade area** — it sells to whoever is within a reasonable drive.

Non-store formats break all three. An online marketplace has an *endless aisle*: adding the 400,000th product costs a database row, not a square foot. It's open at 2 a.m. Its trade area is the shipping map.

But — and this is the part beginners miss — **you don't escape cost, you swap it.** A store's big costs are rent, store labor, and inventory sitting on shelves. A non-store retailer pays little rent, and instead pays for:

- **Customer acquisition** — a store on a busy corner gets foot traffic for free. An online seller buys every visitor through ads, search placement, or a marketplace commission.
- **Fulfillment and the last mile** — picking, packing, and driving one box to one doorstep. A store makes the *customer* do that leg for free.
- **Returns (reverse logistics)** — a shopper who can't touch the product buys two sizes and sends one back. Online return rates run well above in-store rates, and apparel is the worst offender. Each return means shipping paid twice, inspection, repackaging, and often a markdown.

And because the shopper can't touch anything, the retailer must supply **trust substitutes**: photos and video, ratings and reviews, size charts, a generous return policy, a recognizable brand. That's not marketing decoration. It's doing the job the shelf used to do.

One more distinction worth carrying around — **who controls the clock**:

- **TV home shopping** — the *seller* controls it. A scheduled hour, a host demonstrating, a countdown, "only 300 left." You didn't go looking; the format created the demand.
- **Online marketplace** — the *shopper* controls it. You search, filter, compare, and buy on your own schedule. Demand already existed; the retailer competes on price, selection, and delivery speed.
- **Mobile / social commerce** — back to the seller. A feed pushes you something you weren't shopping for, and checkout takes fifteen seconds because your card is already saved.

Which is why **live commerce** — a host demonstrating a product in a live stream with a countdown — isn't new at all. It's TV home shopping, rebuilt on a phone, with a comment section.

## In Everyday Life

It's Sunday, 9 p.m., and you're on the couch in Columbus.

You land on QVC. A host is demonstrating a countertop grill — flipping it open, pressing a sandwich, talking about the removable plates. A counter on screen says how many have sold, and the price is only good for this segment. You weren't shopping for a grill. That's the point: **seller-controlled time, demonstration, urgency.** Home shopping has thrived for decades on categories that are hard to judge from a photo but easy to *show* — kitchen gadgets, jewelry, skincare, mattresses.

You pick up your phone instead and search Amazon for "panini press." Forty results, sorted by review count. You read three one-star reviews, check that it's Prime, and see it arrives Tuesday. **Shopper-controlled time.** Nobody persuaded you of anything; you compared and picked.

Then you open Instagram and a video shows leggings for $34. Two taps, Apple Pay, done, before the video finishes. You never visited a website. In the U.S., most e-commerce traffic now comes through a phone, and checkout friction — not price — is often what decides the sale.

Three retail formats, one couch, twenty minutes.

Now the economics. The leggings don't fit. You get a free return label, drop the bag at the UPS counter inside a Kohl's, and forget about it. For you it cost nothing. For the seller: outbound shipping, return shipping, someone inspecting the bag, and possibly reselling at a discount. That single return can erase the margin on the sale — which is exactly why "free returns" is quietly disappearing at a lot of retailers, and why buy-online-pickup-in-store exists. BOPIS lets the store's building do the last mile for free.

And a number worth keeping in your head: e-commerce is roughly **one in six** U.S. retail dollars, per Census Bureau estimates. Enormous — and also a reminder that about five in six are still spent in a building. Non-store retailing didn't replace stores. It stripped them of their monopoly on selection, hours, and geography, and forced them to compete on the things a warehouse can't do.

## The 3-Line Recap

1. Non-store retailing sells without a sales floor — TV home shopping, online marketplaces, and mobile commerce are its dominant modern forms.
2. It escapes rent, shelf limits, store hours, and trade-area boundaries, but pays for it in customer acquisition, last-mile delivery, and returns.
3. The formats differ by *who controls the clock*: home shopping and social feeds create demand; search-driven marketplaces capture demand that already exists.

## ✅ Self-Quiz

**1.** Which cost is generally *higher* for a pure online retailer than for a comparable physical store?
- (a) Rent per square foot
- (b) In-store labor
- (c) Reverse logistics (handling returns)
- (d) Shrinkage from shoplifting

**2.** TV home shopping and live-stream commerce share the same core mechanic: the seller controls when the product is shown and creates urgency around it. **(O / X)**

**3.** "Endless aisle" refers to:
- (a) A warehouse club's long shelving runs
- (b) An online retailer's ability to list far more SKUs than a store can stock
- (c) A store layout that forces shoppers past every category
- (d) A 24-hour store format

## 📚 Today's Terms

- **Non-store retailing** — selling to final consumers without a fixed physical sales floor: direct selling, vending, catalogs, TV home shopping, e-commerce, and m-commerce.
- **Endless aisle** — the ability to offer a near-unlimited assortment because listings cost data storage rather than shelf space.
- **Customer acquisition cost (CAC)** — what a retailer pays in ads, commissions, or promotions to bring in one buying customer; the online substitute for a good street corner.
- **Last mile** — the final delivery leg from local facility to the customer's door; the most expensive stretch of the supply chain, and the one stores hand to the shopper for free.
- **Reverse logistics** — the process and cost of moving returned goods back, inspecting, restocking, or disposing of them.
- **Live commerce** — real-time video selling with in-stream checkout; structurally, TV home shopping rebuilt for mobile.

---

*Answers: 1 — (c). Without the ability to touch or try the product, online return rates run substantially higher than in-store, especially in apparel, and each return carries shipping, inspection, and markdown costs. 2 — O. Both are seller-controlled time: a scheduled demonstration plus scarcity cues, which generates demand rather than merely capturing it. 3 — (b). "Endless aisle" describes assortment freed from physical shelf constraints; the marginal cost of listing another SKU is close to zero.*
